Area.evidence_source: Of the 44 patients in the chart review, 34 (77%) were characterized as "impulsive." Based on partial information from the narratives of the interviews, the circumstances of the participants' suicide attempts also indicated a high level of impulsivity. Most attempts appeared to be triggered by arguments with significant others or disappointing news related to finances, housing, and employment. All the interviewees made one or more attempts in front of other people or sought help after the attempts. Various methods of suicide were reported in both samples: ingestion of prescription drugs and painkillers, wrist cutting and stabbing of body parts, hanging, and jumping into subway tracks, rivers, or from heights. Different kinds of injury ranging from minimal (superficial cuts) to potential lethality (near-death experiences, loss of speech, and gastrointestinal damage) were incurred. However, there was no pattern of increasing lethality between the various attempts, which could be another indication of the participants' impulsivity.
